links.note: 291 defines truth (வாய்மை) not as reporting what happened but as speech with no harm in it at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). 292 draws the consequence: even a falsehood stands in truth's place (பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த) if it yields faultless good. Read together, the second verse is the first's definition applied to its hardest case.

Both verses use the same question-and-answer frame, எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்: 291 answers that truth is speech with no harm at all, 324 that the good path is the way that keeps in view not killing anything at all. The shared frame shows truthfulness and the good path being defined by the same test, the absence of injury to another.

292 lets a falsehood count as truth when it yields faultless good (புரைதீர்ந்த நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்). 323 ranks not killing as the one good and puts not lying behind it (அதன் பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று). The ranking explains the exception: Parimelazhagar's example for 292 is a lie that saves a creature from death, which is the case where the second virtue gives way to the first.

292 makes good results decisive: a falsehood that yields faultless good (நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்) counts as truth. 113 says gain got by leaving fairness is to be dropped that very day even if it yields nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). The conflict holds only if both are read as answers to whether a good outcome can license a breach of a norm; 113 is about gain and 292 about speech, and 292's புரைதீர்ந்த (free of fault) may already exclude what 113 forbids.

293 forbids lying about what one's own heart knows (தன்நெஞ்சு அறிவது) because that heart will burn one afterwards. 272 asks what a sky-high appearance achieves if one's heart sinks into a fault it knows (தன்னெஞ்சம் தான்அறி குற்றம்). Both make the heart the witness that cannot be deceived, once against the liar and once against the false ascetic.

In 129 a burn from fire heals inside but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not; in 293 the liar's own heart burns him (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both use burning for the lasting damage of speech: the harsh word burns the hearer, the false word burns the speaker.

294 says one who lives without falsehood in the heart (உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யாது) is present in the hearts of all the world. 119 says rectitude is speech without bend, provided there is surely no bend within (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை). In truthfulness and in impartiality alike, straight speech is counted only when the inside matches it.

295 puts one who speaks truth in accord with the mind (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) above those who do austerity together with giving. 160 calls those who fast great, but behind those who bear others' harsh words (இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்). Both rank an everyday discipline of speech, speaking it truly or enduring it, over formal austerity.

295 ranks truthful speech above austerity with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை); 259 says not killing and eating one creature is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின்). The same comparison is made twice: a plain restraint outranks the prestigious religious act.

295 sets the truthful speaker above those who practise austerity and giving. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). In both, the ascetic is the standard of comparison and an ordinary life rightly lived is placed above it.

296 says there is no renown like not lying (பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை). 232 says all that speakers speak is praise resting on those who give to those who ask (இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்). They conflict if both are read as naming the chief ground of renown, truthfulness in one and giving in the other; if 296 is only a chapter's praise of its own virtue the conflict softens.

296 says not lying gives all the virtues (எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்); Parimelazhagar takes எய்யாமை as 'without wearying the body'. 297 then concludes that one who keeps steadily to not lying does well even without doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று). The second verse depends on the first: the others can be left undone because this one already supplies them.

297 says that if one keeps to not lying, not doing other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). 150 says that even if one does not hold to virtue and does wrong, not desiring another's wife is good (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் ... நயவாமை நன்று). Both single out one restraint as worth having even when the rest of virtue is absent.

297 allows that one who never lies may leave the other virtues undone. 181 says that though a man does not speak of virtue and does wrong, it is pleasing to hear it said that he does not backbite (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும் ... புறங்கூறான் என்றல் இனிது). The concession 'even without the rest of virtue' is made for two different restraints of the tongue.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 364 defines purity (தூஉய்மை) as the absence of craving and says that comes by wanting வாய்மை. The later verse gives the inner purity of 298 a content, freedom from desire, and keeps truth as its source.

298 grants that water produces outer purity (புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும்) and assigns inner purity to truth. 278 describes many who bathe as though distinguished while their minds hold dirt (மனத்தது மாசாக ... நீராடி) and live concealed. 278 shows the limit 298 implies: bathing cleans only the outside, and can serve as a cover for the lack of the other purity.

299 says that for the worthy the only lamp is the unfailing lamp (பொய்யா விளக்கே), which in this chapter is not lying. 753 uses the same phrase for wealth: பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம் goes to any land one thinks of and cuts the darkness. The Book of Virtue denies the name of lamp to everything but truthfulness, and the Book of Wealth gives the same title to money.

299 names not lying the one true lamp for the worthy (பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு). 601 calls lineage an undimming lamp (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) that nevertheless goes out when the grime of sloth covers it. The lamp figure marks what a person's standing depends on, and 601 adds that such a lamp can be put out by neglect.

300 says that among all the things we have seen as true there is nothing whatever better than truthfulness (எனைத்தொன்றும் வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற இல்லை). 323 says the one good is not killing and that not lying is good behind it (அதன் பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று). On the plain reading the two verses rank the same pair of virtues in opposite order.

300 speaks in the first person plural: 'among what we have seen as true' (யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள்) nothing is better than truthfulness. 61 uses the same voice: 'of all that can be gained we know of nothing' (யாமறிவது இல்லை) like children who know what should be known. In both the author steps forward with 'we' to vouch for a superlative, which the Kural seldom does.

301 says only one who holds back anger where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான்) truly holds it back; Parimelazhagar takes this as anger at those weaker. 250 gives the means: when going against one weaker than yourself (தன்னின் மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து), think of yourself standing before the stronger. 301 says where restraint counts, and 250 supplies the thought that makes it possible.

301 counts restraint of anger only where the anger could have its way. 153 says the strength of strengths is bearing with fools (வன்மையுள் வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை). Both locate the real test of forbearance where one has the upper hand and nothing outside compels it.

302 says anger is bad where it cannot take effect, and where it can, nothing is worse (செல்லிடத்தும் இல்அதனின் தீய பிற); Parimelazhagar reads the two places as the stronger and the weaker. 861 advises avoiding opposition to the strong and pressing enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). They conflict if 302 is taken as a rule for everyone; if the anger chapter is addressed to ascetics, as Parimelazhagar holds, and 861 to a king, they are advice for different people.

302's first half says anger where it cannot take effect is bad, which Parimelazhagar explains as harm coming back from the stronger party. 895 states that harm at its extreme: those a king of fierce might is angry with (வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) will not survive wherever they go. The chapter on not offending the great fills in what 302 leaves as a bare 'bad'.

152 says always bear with an excess done to you, and that forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 303 uses the same verb for the anger itself: forget anger toward anyone (மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும்), since evils are born from it. One forgets the offence and the other the anger at it; 303 adds the reason.

303 says evils are born from anger (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). 360 names anger (வெகுளி) with desire and confusion as the three whose very names must perish for pain to perish. What 303 says of anger as a source of evils, 360 places in a full account of the roots of suffering.

304 asks whether there is any other enemy than anger, which kills the smile and the joy (சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற). 165 says envy is enough for the envious: even if enemies fail, it brings ruin (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). Both treat an inner fault as an enemy that needs no outside enemy to finish the work.

304 counts the death of laughter and joy (நகையும் உவகையும்) as the harm that makes anger the worst enemy. 999 says that for those not capable of laughing (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு) the great world lies in darkness even by day. 999 describes the state that 304 says anger produces.

305 and 127 are built on the same turn, காக்க ... காவாக்கால்: guard against anger, or it is yourself that anger kills; guard the tongue whatever else you leave unguarded, or you will suffer from the fault of your words. In both, the thing to be guarded is something of one's own, and the one who fails to guard it is the one harmed.

305 says one who would guard himself (தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின்) must guard against anger. 209 says one who loves himself (தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின்) should not go near evil deeds, however small. Both argue from self-interest alone: the restraint is recommended as self-protection, not as a duty to others.

306 says anger, the fire that kills what it adjoins (சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி), burns even the safe raft of one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 526 says no one on earth has more people around him than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). The two give the loss and the gain of the same fact: kin stay with the one who is free of anger.

306 calls one's people a safe raft (ஏமப் புணை) that anger burns. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love certainly exists and the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. The same phrase names what keeps a person afloat; in one verse a passion destroys it and in the other a passion leaves the speaker without one.

307 says the ruin of one who takes anger for a thing of worth is as sure as the hand of one who strikes the ground, which cannot miss (நிலத்தறைந்தான் கைபிழையாதற்று). 208 says the ruin of evildoers is like a shadow that stays at one's foot and never leaves (நிழல்தன்னை வீயாது அடிஉறைந்தற்று). Both use a plain physical certainty to say the consequence cannot be escaped; Kalaignar reads 307 as adding that the striking hand is what gets hurt.

308 says that even if someone does harm like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்), not being angry is good, if one can manage it (புணரின்). 312 says that even when someone has done hurt in hatred, not doing hurt in return is the settled stand of the stainless (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை). 308 governs the feeling and 312 the act that would follow from it; 308 alone concedes that it may not be possible.

308 asks for no anger even under harm like fire. 852, in the chapter on hostility in the Book of Wealth, says that even if someone does what cannot be borne, meaning division, not doing harm in return is best (இன்னா செய்யாமை தலை). The same advice, with the same 'even if ... செயினும்' form, is given as virtue in one book and as policy in the other.

309 says all one has thought of is gained at once (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்) if one never thinks of anger in the heart. 540 says gaining what one has thought of is easy (உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது) if one can keep thinking of it. Both promise the same result in nearly the same words and set a condition on the mind: one removes a thought, the other holds one.

265 says austerity is striven for here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 309 says all that is thought of is obtained if anger is never thought of; Parimelazhagar takes its subject to be the one doing austerity. On that reading 309 names the condition under which the promise of 265 holds.

309 praises one who does not think of anger in the heart at all (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly on the spot but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). They conflict if both describe how a wise person treats anger inwardly, one removing it and the other keeping it for later; the conflict lessens if 309 is for the ascetic, as Parimelazhagar reads it, and 487 for a ruler facing enemies.

310 plays on இறந்தார் and துறந்தார்: those who go beyond bounds in anger are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are the equals of the renounced. 159 uses the same two words: those who bear harsh words from the mouths of இறந்தார் (those who overstep) have the purity of துறந்தார். In both, a householder's control over anger is measured against the renouncer and found equal.

310 makes giving up anger the mark that puts one level with renouncers (சினத்தைத் துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை). 29, in the chapter on the greatness of renouncers, speaks of the anger of those who stand on the hill of good qualities (குன்றேறி நின்றார் வெகுளி). On Pope's and Parimelazhagar's reading of 29, that this anger cannot be withstood even for a moment, the great renouncers do get angry; on the other reading, that they cannot keep anger even for a moment, the two verses agree.
